intro.title: Discover Willow Creek Hoodoos
intro.entityIntro: Welcome to Willow Creek Hoodoos (Drumheller), the iconic sandstone hoodoo formation recognised worldwide as a must-visit scenic spot in Alberta's Canadian Badlands. Located in the heart of Drumheller, Alberta, Canada, this destination serves as a primary stop for travellers exploring the Drumheller Valley and the wider Alberta Badlands.
intro.description:
Willow Creek Hoodoos is a spectacular scenic spot located near Drumheller, Alberta, Canada. This natural landmark features unique hoodoo rock formations created by centuries of erosion and weathering.

Hoodoos are tall, thin rock spires that rise from the ground, formed by differential erosion of sedimentary rock. These fascinating geological structures are the result of thousands of years of natural forces shaping the landscape.

Located along Coulee Way in the heart of the Canadian Badlands, Willow Creek Hoodoos offers visitors a chance to witness these incredible natural sculptures up close and learn about the geological history of Alberta's prairie region.

knowledge.title: About Willow Creek Hoodoos
knowledge.subtitle: A concise, science-based introduction to the geology, history and legends of the Drumheller Badlands, written by an independent nonprofit educational project.

sections.title: Geological Formation — Rocks 68-72 Million Years Old
sections.content:
The pillars of Willow Creek Hoodoos are carved from the Horseshoe Canyon Formation, a stack of Late Cretaceous river deposits laid down between about 68 and 72 million years ago. At the time, Drumheller lay on a vast, warm floodplain beside an inland sea: floods dumped sand, silt and mud, swamps became thin coal seams, and buried channels hardened into the sandstones you see today.

Look closely at a hoodoo and you are reading a vertical slice of a vanished world — every band is one ancient flood. The rock itself may be 70 million years old, yet the elegant spire shape is far younger, sculpted only within the last few thousand years by ice, wind and water.

sections.title: How Hoodoos Form — Caps, Frost and Rain
sections.content:
Every hoodoo starts with a cap. A harder, resistant rock — often an iron-cemented sandstone — sits on top like an umbrella, shielding the softer claystone and siltstone column beneath. Rain and meltwater roll off the cap's rim, while wind-borne grit and the freeze-thaw cycle attack the exposed pedestal, narrowing it year after year.

Geologists call this differential erosion. It produces the classic hoodoo silhouette: wider at the top, slimmer at the waist. Alberta's winters matter enormously here — water seeping into cracks freezes, expands and pries the rock apart. When a cap finally overhangs too far it cracks and falls, and the unprotected column erodes away quickly. Hoodoos are born, age and topple on a human timescale, so the view changes with every generation.

sections.title: A Young Landscape Carved by Ice
sections.content:
Although the bedrock is tens of millions of years old, the valley around Willow Creek Hoodoos is young. During the last ice age the Laurentide Ice Sheet covered much of Alberta; as the ice retreated roughly 12,000-16,000 years ago, torrents of meltwater sliced deep coulees and the Willow Creek valley into the plains.

That is why the Badlands feel both ancient and restless. Bare sandstone can lose centimetres in a single flash flood, and every spring thaw reshapes the slopes. Standing at the lookout, you are inside a landscape that is still being made.

sections.title: Location & Access
sections.content:
Willow Creek Hoodoos is located along Coulee Way in Drumheller, Alberta, Canada. The site is easily accessible by car, with a paid parking lot at the Hoodoos site during the Town of Drumheller's designated visitor season (check the Town of Drumheller visitor parking page for current rates). Coordinates are approximately 51.3806° N, 112.5342° W (Google Maps plus code 9FJ8+78 Drumheller, Alberta, Canada).

Drumheller is known as the 'Dinosaur Capital of the World' and is located about 135 kilometres northeast of Calgary. The hoodoos are one of the many natural attractions in the area, alongside the Royal Tyrrell Museum of Palaeontology, the Hoodoo Trail and Dinosaur Provincial Park.

sections.title: Dinosaur Country — Fossils All Around
sections.content:
The coulees around Willow Creek Hoodoos cut through some of the world's richest dinosaur-bearing rock. In the Late Cretaceous these river plains teemed with life, and the very sediments that built the hoodoos entombed countless animals. Drumheller's formations have yielded duck-billed hadrosaurs, armoured ankylosaurs and the predatory Albertosaurus — the 'Alberta lizard' named after this province.

This fossil wealth earned Drumheller the title 'Dinosaur Capital of the World'. The Royal Tyrrell Museum of Palaeontology, a short drive away, displays skeletons from these very rocks, and its outdoor and outreach programmes help explain the Badlands that surround the hoodoos. If you spot what looks like bone, leave it in place and tell the museum: every fossil in the Badlands is a protected scientific record.

sections.title: Indigenous Heritage and the Coal-Town Era
sections.content:
The Drumheller valley lies within the traditional territory of the Niitsitapi (Blackfoot) peoples — the Siksika, Kainai and Piikani Nations — along with the Stoney Nakoda, Tsuut'ina and Metis peoples who have travelled these coulees for millennia. Hoodoos served as landmarks and campsites, and their meaning lives on in oral tradition.

After the railway arrived in the 1880s, Drumheller's thick coal seams turned the valley into one of Canada's busiest mining towns, attracting miners from across Europe and from Chinese Canadian communities. The mines closed by the 1970s, but the railway town, the museum and reclaimed trails still tell that story today. Willow Creek Hoodoos is stewarded together with the Town of Drumheller and Alberta Parks as part of this shared heritage.

sections.title: Legends, Folklore and the Name 'Hoodoo'
sections.content:
Wherever hoodoos rise, stories follow. Several Indigenous oral traditions of the Northern Plains describe the stone pillars as petrified giants or spirit beings — in some tellings, ancient people were turned to stone and still watch over the valley. Later settlers, seeing silhouettes shift at dusk, nicknamed them 'tent rocks' and traded fireside tales that the pillars crept about at night.

The English word 'hoodoo' travelled west in the 1800s from folk usage connected with 'voodoo' and was applied to the strangely magical rock towers of the Canadian and American West. Legends differ, but they share one idea: the Willow Creek Hoodoos feel alive — and deserve the respect of every visitor.

sections.title: Preservation & Leave No Trace
sections.content:
Hoodoos are fragile natural structures that can be damaged by human activity. Climbing on or touching the hoodoos is strictly prohibited to preserve these geological wonders for future generations.

Visitors are asked to stay on designated pathways and respect all signage. The Town of Drumheller and Alberta Parks work together to maintain the site and educate visitors about the importance of preserving these unique natural formations at Willow Creek Hoodoos.

faq.title: Willow Creek Hoodoos — Frequently Asked Questions
faq.subtitle: Answers to the most common questions about visiting Willow Creek Hoodoos (Drumheller, Alberta).

items.question: What are the hoodoos in Alberta?
items.answer: The hoodoos of Alberta are tall, thin sandstone pillars capped with harder rock. Over millions of years, wind and water eroded the softer sandstone beneath the caps, leaving these otherworldly formations standing. Willow Creek Hoodoos, in the Canadian Badlands near Drumheller, is one of the most photographed examples of this landscape.

items.question: How were the Willow Creek Hoodoos formed?
items.answer: The Willow Creek Hoodoos began as layers of sediment laid down in an ancient river valley about 70 million years ago. Over time, weathering and erosion wore away the valley floor, while harder caprock shielded the softer sandstone beneath it - leaving the mushroom-shaped pillars visible today.

items.question: Where is Willow Creek Hoodoos located?
items.answer: Willow Creek Hoodoos is located along Coulee Way in Drumheller, Alberta, Canada (Google Maps plus code 9FJ8+78 Drumheller, Alberta), in the heart of the Canadian Badlands. The geographic coordinates are approximately 51.3806° N, 112.5342° W.

items.question: Is Willow Creek Hoodoos free to visit?
items.answer: Yes. Willow Creek Hoodoos is a public scenic spot and entry is free of charge year-round. Visitors can walk the interpretive trail around the hoodoos from dawn to dusk without paying an entrance fee.

items.question: How long is the Willow Creek Hoodoos hike and how difficult is it?
items.answer: The Willow Creek Hoodoos hike is a short, family-friendly loop of roughly 1–2 kilometres. Plan about 60–90 minutes to walk the trail, photograph the hoodoos and read the interpretive signs. Sturdy shoes are recommended as the terrain is uneven.

items.question: What is the best time of year or day to visit Willow Creek Hoodoos?
items.answer: Late spring through mid-autumn (May to October) is the best window, with sunrise and sunset providing the softest light on the sandstone pillars. Winter visits are possible but bring warm layers; the snow-capped hoodoos are especially photogenic.

items.question: What other attractions are near Willow Creek Hoodoos in Drumheller?
items.answer: From Willow Creek Hoodoos you can easily reach the Royal Tyrrell Museum of Palaeontology, drive the famous Hoodoo Trail, hike Horseshoe Canyon, or continue along the Dinosaur Trail to the Atlas Coal Mine National Historic Site — all within roughly 30 minutes of Drumheller.

items.question: Can I climb the hoodoos or take rocks home?
items.answer: No. Climbing the hoodoos, removing rocks, and stepping off the designated paths are strictly prohibited to protect the fragile sandstone formations. Willow Creek Hoodoos is jointly stewarded by the Town of Drumheller and Alberta Parks.

items.question: Where can I park when visiting Willow Creek Hoodoos?
items.answer: Paid parking applies at the Hoodoos lot during the Town of Drumheller's designated visitor season. The lot sits along Coulee Way directly beside the trailhead and fits cars, RVs and tour buses. Rates and payment instructions change by season, so check current details on the Town of Drumheller visitor parking page before you arrive: https://www.drumheller.ca/live/pay-parking/visitor-parking

items.question: Are there washrooms or restrooms near Willow Creek Hoodoos?
items.answer: There are no permanent public washrooms directly at the Willow Creek Hoodoos trailhead. The nearest public facilities are in Drumheller town centre and at visitor-serving stops along the drive from town, so plan your washroom stops before heading onto the trail.

items.question: Where can visitors find food, fuel and lodging near Willow Creek Hoodoos?
items.answer: Drumheller town centre, roughly 10-15 minutes by car, offers a full range of services by type: family restaurants, cafes and fast food; grocery stores and convenience shops; hotels, motels, bed-and-breakfasts and RV campgrounds; plus fuel stations and electric-vehicle charging points. As a nonprofit science guide we describe categories only and do not promote individual businesses — please check current opening hours and availability before travelling.

items.title: Public Washrooms
items.text: There are no permanent public washrooms at the Willow Creek Hoodoos trailhead. The nearest public facilities are in Drumheller town centre and at visitor-serving stops along the drive from town. Plan your washroom stops before the trail.

items.title: Parking & Vehicle Access
items.text: Paid parking applies at the Hoodoos lot during the Town of Drumheller's designated visitor season. The lot sits along Coulee Way beside the trailhead and fits cars, RVs and tour buses. Rates and payment change by season, so confirm current details on the Town of Drumheller visitor parking page before you arrive. The final stretch of road is paved; in winter, check for ice before driving.

items.title: Dining & Picnic Options
items.text: Drumheller town centre, roughly 10-15 minutes away, offers family restaurants, cafes, fast food, bakeries and pizzerias. For a scenic meal, bring your own food and water — and always carry out your litter.

items.title: Lodging & Camping
items.text: By type, the Drumheller Valley offers hotels, motels, bed-and-breakfasts, inns, RV parks and campgrounds, concentrated in town and along the main access highways. Book ahead in summer and during dinosaur-themed events.

items.title: Groceries & Supplies
items.text: Supermarkets, grocery stores and convenience shops are located in Drumheller town centre. Stock up on water, snacks, sunscreen and ice before heading into the Badlands, where services are limited.

items.title: Fuel & EV Charging

meta.title: Drumheller Day Trip: Royal Tyrrell Museum & Willow Creek Hoodoos
meta.description: Plan the classic Drumheller day trip: pair the Royal Tyrrell Museum of Palaeontology with a short hike to Willow Creek Hoodoos, with route, timing, family and photography tips.

drumhellerDayTrip.pageTitle: Drumheller Day Trip: Royal Tyrrell Museum + Willow Creek Hoodoos
drumhellerDayTrip.standfirst: The two essential stops on most Drumheller itineraries are the Royal Tyrrell Museum of Palaeontology and the Willow Creek Hoodoos: one indoors, one outdoors, roughly 15-20 minutes apart by car. This page lays out how to combine them for a half-day or full-day trip, written as a neutral orientation guide.

sections.heading: Suggested order: morning museum, late-afternoon hoodoos (or the reverse)
paragraphs: Start at the Royal Tyrrell Museum, set in Midland Provincial Park on the western edge of Drumheller. Mornings tend to be calmer in summer before school groups and tour buses arrive, and the air-conditioned galleries make a comfortable midday option.

Head to Willow Creek Hoodoos later in the day, when the lower sun brings out the contrast of the sandstone pillars. Alternatively, visit the hoodoos first at sunrise and take your time in the museum afterwards. Both orders work well.

sections.heading: What to budget for each stop
paragraphs: Royal Tyrrell Museum: most visitors spend 2-3 hours indoors (the galleries plus the Fossil Preparation Lab viewing area). Admission is ticketed and, during summer and school breaks, booking ahead on the museum's official website is recommended. We do not publish prices here because they change seasonally - always confirm on the official site.

Willow Creek Hoodoos: the open-air site is free and accessible year-round. Allow 30-60 minutes to walk the trail and viewpoints, or longer for photography. Paid parking applies at the Hoodoos lot during the visitor season — confirm current rates on the Town of Drumheller parking page.

sections.heading: Doing it with kids
paragraphs: The museum's dinosaur galleries are a natural draw for children, and the hoodoos offer plenty of space to stretch legs safely on the marked trail. Keep children close at viewpoints near soft cliff edges, carry water and sun protection in summer, and plan bathroom stops in town - there are no washroom buildings directly at the hoodoos site.

sections.heading: Adding more around Drumheller
paragraphs: If you have time, the Hoodoo Trail viewpoints along the south side of the valley, Horseshoe Canyon, the Atlas Coal Mine National Historic Site and Drumheller's dinosaur-themed street decor all sit within easy reach. See our by-area guide to food, groceries and services if you plan to eat or stock up on the way.

foodAndServices.pageTitle: Food, Groceries & Services Near Willow Creek Hoodoos
foodAndServices.standfirst: This page is an objective orientation guide to food, groceries and practical services around Willow Creek Hoodoos and Drumheller. Following the editorial policy of this site, we list categories and neighbourhoods only and do not recommend or rank any individual business. Opening hours change seasonally, so always confirm details directly before you set out.

sections.heading: By neighbourhood
paragraphs: Drumheller town centre: the main street and bridge-end area hold the largest cluster of restaurants, cafés, fast-food and grocery options, roughly 10-15 minutes by car from the hoodoos site.
Rosedale and the Willow Creek coulee side: the closest options to the site itself are few but practical - mostly convenience and quick-service choices near the highway approach to Coulee Way.
The Dinosaur Trail / Highway 9 corridor: a mix of roadside services and family-style dining spaced along the drive between Drumheller and the valley's other attractions.
East Coulee and beyond: heading south-east on Highway 838, expect a small-community scale of services rather than a full commercial strip.

sections.heading: What to expect by type
paragraphs: Sit-down dining: family restaurants and steakhouses are the common style in and around Drumheller; most cluster in town rather than at the hoodoos themselves.
Quick service and takeaway: fast-food and drive-thru options concentrate in town and along the main highway approaches.
Cafés, bakeries and ice cream: available mainly in the town centre; summer is the busy season.
Groceries and convenience: full supermarkets are in town; convenience stores and gas-station shops are the practical option closer to the coulee area.
Picnic supplies: if you plan a picnic at the hoodoos, note there are no food vendors directly at the site - buy water and snacks before you arrive.

sections.heading: Seasonal planning tips
paragraphs: May to October is the high season, when most places open longer hours; outside that, hours can shorten significantly, so check before visiting on weekdays or off-season.
At lunchtime in summer the busiest options in town fill up; consider eating earlier or later if you are on a tight itinerary.

parkingAndDirections.standfirst: Practical directions for reaching Willow Creek Hoodoos, the paid parking at the site, and how to plan the drive from Calgary or Drumheller town centre.

sections.heading: Getting there from Drumheller town centre
paragraphs: Willow Creek Hoodoos is about a 10-15 minute drive from downtown Drumheller. Follow the signs to the Hoodoo Trail (Highway 10) and then to 'Hoodoos'; the site sits along Coulee Way on the south side of the valley.

The final approach is paved and suitable for cars, RVs and tour buses. There is no public transit to the site, so driving or joining a guided tour from Calgary or Drumheller is the most reliable option.

sections.heading: From Calgary (YYC)
paragraphs: Drive about 1.5-2 hours from Calgary. Take Highway 2 North, then Highway 9 East to Drumheller, and follow signs to the Hoodoo Trail. From the Calgary airport (YYC) allow closer to 2 hours with rental-car pick-up and summer traffic.
It is an easy half-day or full-day loop: pair the Hoodoos with the Royal Tyrrell Museum, which is roughly 15-20 minutes away by car.

sections.heading: Parking at the site
paragraphs: Paid parking applies at the Hoodoos lot during the Town of Drumheller's designated visitor season. The lot sits along Coulee Way directly beside the trailhead and fits cars, RVs and tour buses.
Rates and payment instructions change by season. Confirm current details on the Town of Drumheller visitor parking page before you set off, and carry a payment method that works at the lot.

sections.heading: Tips for RVs, buses and families
paragraphs: The lot and access road are paved, but the trail surface is uneven gravel — sturdy shoes are recommended and the trail is not step-free. In peak summer the lot fills early, so arrive in the morning.
There are no permanent public washrooms at the trailhead. Plan restroom stops in Drumheller town centre before you arrive, and carry water, especially on hot days.

hoodoosTrailGuide.standfirst: Everything you need to know about walking the Willow Creek Hoodoos trail — distance, surface, viewpoints and the best light for photography.

sections.heading: Trail at a glance
paragraphs: The Willow Creek Hoodoos walk is a short, family-friendly loop of roughly 1-2 kilometres. Plan about 60-90 minutes to walk the trail, photograph the hoodoos and read the interpretive signs.
The surface is uneven, loose gravel with a few steps near the viewpoint. It is not step-free, so wear sturdy footwear and take care with children and strollers.

sections.heading: Highlights along the route
paragraphs: Start at the parking area on Coulee Way and follow the designated pathway to the main viewing platform, which looks out over the cluster of hoodoos and the Badlands beyond.
Interpretive signs along the trail explain how the sandstone pillars formed, and the close-up rock faces show the sedimentary layers that record an ancient river floodplain.

sections.heading: Best time to walk
paragraphs: Late spring through mid-autumn (May to October) is the most comfortable window, with sunrise and sunset giving the softest light on the sandstone. Summer afternoons are hot and the trail has almost no shade.
In winter the hoodoos dusted with snow are especially photogenic, but the path can be icy — wear non-slip boots and walk slowly.

sections.heading: Trail etiquette & safety
paragraphs: Stay on the marked pathway and never climb the hoodoos or remove rocks — the sandstone is fragile and protected. Keep back from the soft cliff edges at the viewpoint.
Weather in the coulees changes fast. Check the forecast, carry water and sun protection, and postpone the walk if thunderstorms are forecast.

meta.title: Things to Do in Drumheller Near the Hoodoos
meta.description: Beyond the Hoodoos: the Royal Tyrrell Museum, Hoodoo Trail, Horseshoe Canyon, Atlas Coal Mine and family activities in Drumheller, Alberta.

thingsToDoInDrumheller.standfirst: A neutral orientation guide to the top things to do around Drumheller, paired with your visit to Willow Creek Hoodoos.

sections.heading: Royal Tyrrell Museum of Palaeontology
paragraphs: The Royal Tyrrell Museum is one of the world's premier palaeontology museums, about 15-20 minutes from the Hoodoos. Most visitors spend 2-3 hours indoors among dinosaur skeletons and the fossil preparation lab.

Admission is ticketed and, in summer and school breaks, booking ahead on the museum's official website is recommended. We do not publish prices because they change seasonally — confirm on the official site.

sections.heading: Hoodoo Trail & roadside viewpoints
paragraphs: The Hoodoo Trail (Highway 10) is a scenic drive with pull-offs and viewpoints over the Badlands. Willow Creek Hoodoos is the most developed stop, but several roadside viewpoints are worth a short stop.
Allow extra time if you want to string together multiple viewpoints rather than just the main Hoodoos lot.

sections.heading: Horseshoe Canyon
paragraphs: Horseshoe Canyon is a dramatic, layered canyon about 15-20 minutes from Drumheller with a viewpoint and a steep trail into the coulees. It is a good add-on for photography and a short hike.
The descent is strenuous and exposed — the rim viewpoint alone is rewarding if you are short on time.

sections.heading: Atlas Coal Mine National Historic Site
paragraphs: The Atlas Coal Mine National Historic Site tells the story of Drumheller's coal-mining era, with guided tours and a restored tipple. It sits about 20-25 minutes east of town.
Tour availability is seasonal, so check ahead if a guided experience is part of your plan.

sections.heading: Family & rainy-day options
paragraphs: On hot or wet days, lean on indoor stops: the Royal Tyrrell Museum, the Drumheller Museum and the town's dinosaur-themed street decor keep kids engaged.
Drumheller town centre (10-15 minutes away) has restaurants, cafés, grocery stores, fuel and lodging by type — see our food & services guide for a neutral overview.

officialManagement.title: About Willow Creek Hoodoos (Drumheller)
officialManagement.text: Willow Creek Hoodoos is a free, year-round scenic stop on the south side of the Drumheller Valley, about 10-15 minutes from town and 15-20 minutes from the Royal Tyrrell Museum. The site has a paved access road, a paid parking lot in season, an interpretive trail loop of roughly 1-2 km, and a viewing platform over the hoodoos. Plan 30-90 minutes, wear sturdy shoes, and check the weather before you set out.
